title: Anyone can build it with AI; the difference is depth
introduction: No class on Tuesday this week. Boyd called us into his office one by one for a short personal-tutor check-in, and the rest of the day was ours to prepare for Thursday's crit. Wednesday is Ross's first Python workshop, and Thursday is the Project 1 crit with a guest artist, Orna, who works with holograms, immersive projection and 3D printing. So this post is not about code. It is about a twenty-minute conversation and what I decided because of it.
related_work: Boyd set out the rest of the term. The crit on Thursday is not about a perfect project: 'it's about getting you a project that you can continue to develop, identifying the gaps in knowledge.' After this week the module moves into projection mapping, with TouchDesigner, Unity and Blender, towards real-time visuals that respond to sound and to the room. The Python workshops run alongside, without pressure, with the proper start next week.
method: In the one-to-one I told him the truth about how Project 0 and Project 1 went. Both times I changed the plan close to the deadline and then drew a large number of new images in two or three days, and both times my sleep fell apart. I came in with no coding background and have been using AI as a teacher; the Project 1 code was easier than Project 0 because I found a paper and a p5 demo to build on. Boyd's reply was short. He said I am progressing well, and that his way of teaching is exactly this: make a large project first, with AI if necessary, and go back for the technique afterwards. Then he gave me two rules for Project 2 and 3. Slow down at the start and 'work in a more prototype fashion': use any image grabbed from the web as a placeholder, and only make original material once the concept is fixed. And 'allow your initial work to be ugly': fast, rough and ugly until the idea works, and make it beautiful last. The sentence that stayed with me was this one: with AI, anyone can now make a website or a game. What cannot be generated is an interesting, critical concept. That is where the value is.
results_discussion: So I asked myself the uncomfortable question about Project 1. What is it, honestly? Two strangers, a camera each, a hand gesture each, and a childhood that assembles itself out of silhouettes and a picture book whose colours run away like sand. It is warm, and warmth is the problem. Nothing in it makes anyone want to argue. A childhood piece becomes critical only when it says something about how we remember, not what we remember. Looking at it again, the argument was already inside the work; I just had not said it out loud. First: the childhood on screen is written in the present. Two people who never met use today's mood to compose a past that neither of them lived, and it still looks true. Memory is not retrieved, it is reconstructed, which is what Bartlett found in 1932 and what Boym calls reflective nostalgia: a longing that knows it is making things up. Second: the silhouettes let everyone recognise themselves only because every detail has been removed. A shared childhood exists on the condition that the specific people and places are erased. This is exactly the shadow in Plato's cave that Sean Cubitt returned to in Tuesday's projection lecture: we take the shadow for the thing. The game is deliberately crude: win, lose and draw become happy, sad and calm, because that is all a child's day is made of, and because that is all an adult remembers of it. So the sentence I will stand behind on Thursday is this: childhood is not found; it is co-written in the present, by two people, out of shadows. The code will go on GitHub after the crit; the ten minutes should be about that sentence.
conclusion_future_work: For Project 2 I only have a direction, not a method: a flock or a particle system in TouchDesigner, projected, responding to sound. I do not yet know how it will be made, and after this conversation I think that is the right place to be in week 7. The order will change from Project 1. First the concept and the critical question, sent to Boyd by email before anything is produced. Then the whole pipeline run through with placeholder images, so that the code is understood before it is beautiful. Original material comes last, in one go. The aim is a project that I can explain for ten minutes without once mentioning how it was built.
